title: Towards Controlled Chemical and Electrochemical Reactivity during In Situ Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy
content: Liquid phase (scanning) transmission electron microscopy, LP-(S)TEM, has opened new possibilities in materials science by enabling real-time, nanoscale imaging of specimens under environmental conditions. The development of advanced liquid holders capable of setting varying flow rates and applying an electrical bias has allowed in situ characterization of electroactive materials. Despite these advances, in situ electrochemical scanning transmission electron microscopy, EC-STEM, remains challenging. For instance, data collection and interpretation can be complicated by artefacts stemming from on-chip electrode geometry, liquid-phase confinement and electron beam irradiation, among others [1]. Generally, chemical and electrochemical processes in EC experiments are often intertwined, making the control of the reactivity complex; and this is particularly true for EC-STEM experiments. For instance, halide salts such as KCl and NaCl are commonly used as supporting electrolytes to increase the ionic strength of the solution and lower the Ohmic drop. While these additives help controlling electrochemical reactivity, halides are also known to alter the oxidizing/reducing power of radicals and molecules produced in the electron beam-induced radiolysis of aqueous solutions as well as to scavenge OH⋅ radicals, thus affecting chemical reactivity [2]. Specific to EC-STEM, mass transport in small volume cells can also be a limiting factor, altering the reactivity.
